messages.author: da6d9613ff0dac62
messages.subject: Parallel growth model
parts: Hello, I’m trying to run a parallel growth model, which can be done in Mplus. Would this be the same as a multilevel sem in lavaan? Or is there a special function for it?

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
parts:
Hello, 

This can be done with the growth() function (which really just calls on the lavaan() function). This is not the same as multilevel sem.

for three time points, intercept and slope only, this would look like: 


model <-
'
Intercept1 =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3
slope1 =~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3

Intercept2 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3
slope2 =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3

'

fit<- growth(model, data = dat)
summary(fit)

pay attention to your covariances if you have specific specifications (e.g., intercept predicting slope), but this will have all latent vars covary and have estimated variances by default.

Thank you so much for this! I don’t believe I have any covariances restrictions what I really want to see is if two growth models are interacting (I.e. changing at the same rate either in the same or opposite directions) so I assume that if I leave the model with this code I will obtain this information with the covariances right?

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
parts:
Yes, latent variables automatically are given a variance and a covariance which you'll see. 

If you want a significance test to see if the rate is significantly different (if that matters to you at all, it might not, but it sounds like this might be what you're doing), you'll have to be creative though. 

In particular you'd want to specify a model which had no constraints on the slope (i.e., what I wrote above), then another model which constrains them to be the same, then you'd do a lavTestLRT(fit1, fit2) call on the two fitted objects. If the test is significant, then you'd prefer the model without the constraint, which would say the slopes are significantly different, otherwise they are not significantly different.

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
parts:
You're close, you constrained them to be the same, but also constrained them to be 0, which you don't want if I'm understanding you correctly. That is a good model to compare intercept-only to intercept and slope growth.

If you're specifically looking to test if the two slopes are significantly different from one another (or technically, if the model fits significantly better when they're specified separately or not), you will do the unconstrained PPM like above, then the constrained PPM.

You'll want to set the slopes to be equal with a label (both the same label), like this: 

constrainedMod <-

'
Intercept1 =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3
slope1 =~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3

Intercept2 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3
slope2 =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3

s1~constraint*1
s2~constraint*1

'
then do an lavTestLRT(unconstrainedMod, constrainedMod). The null hypothesis of this test is essentially that the models fit the same, if so, pick the one with more df because its parsimonious. 

Regarding fit measures, there's an entire literature on this. Hu & Bentler 1999 is often cited, but there are papers about how incremental fit indices are poorer for growth curves. In my own work, I typically have had growth curves fit the Hu & Bentler criteria, though. The importance of fit is related to how important accurate interpretations are. Fit tells you if the model you impose is reflected in the data.

Freed timepoints can be compared to fixed timepoints with lavTestLRT() as well. Models can be more complex that way and you will need some SEM knowlegde to interpret correctly, but if you have more than 3 waves of data it's possible.

Explore this youtube channel for theoretical understanding of some of your questions: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7kcXN1Xoj4PzMIKPHJ5m7Q/videos

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
parts:
Hi.

First, please include your lavaan() call.

Warning 1: What are the raw-data scales for WP and PRE?

Having observed variables with widely varying metrics can cause
computational problems. Look at descriptive statistics for your
observed variables. If the variances of some of the variables are much
larger (lavaan says >1000x) than the variances of the others. One
possibility to check is if you have some numeric missing value flags
(e.g., 999 on a 1-5 scale).

If the values are correct, the usual practice is to divide the values
of the large one by a constant to bring the variances in line. This
will not affect statistical conclusions from the model, though you may
need to go back and rescale the unstandardized parameter estimates
afterward if the resulting scaling is not intuitive.

Fixing this can sometimes help with the NPD error, so I'd try it first.

As for Warning 2, it is what it says it is. You've got an N of 16,
possibly in just one group (again, you haven't sent the lavaan call).
What missing data method did you specify? If you didn't specify, I
think the default is listwise deletion, so you've lost most of your
sample.

Pat

Em domingo, 5 de julho de 2020 22:52:00 UTC+10, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) escreveu:

Hi.

First, please include your lavaan() call.

Warning 1: What are the raw-data scales for WP and PRE?

Having observed variables with widely varying metrics can cause
computational problems. Look at descriptive statistics for your
observed variables. If the variances of some of the variables are much
larger (lavaan says >1000x) than the variances of the others. One
possibility to check is if you have some numeric missing value flags
(e.g., 999 on a 1-5 scale).

If the values are correct, the usual practice is to divide the values
of the large one by a constant to bring the variances in line. This
will not affect statistical conclusions from the model, though you may
need to go back and rescale the unstandardized parameter estimates
afterward if the resulting scaling is not intuitive.

Fixing this can sometimes help with the NPD error, so I'd try it first.

As for Warning 2, it is what it says it is. You've got an N of 16,
possibly in just one group (again, you haven't sent the lavaan call).
What missing data method did you specify? If you didn't specify, I
think the default is listwise deletion, so you've lost most of your
sample.

Pat

Ok. If the N really is 16, that is your problem, and it's what lavaan
is telling you is the problem.

Your larger model is almost certainly empirically underidentified.
It's not specific to lavaan. That's probably also why you have the NPD
error.

For some of your other questions:
"Is it ok if one variable is divided by 10 and another by 1000 for example?"

Yes. Linear transformations such as addition and division by a
constant do not affect the substantive results, but can make
computations easier.

Order of variables does not matter.

I'm not familiar with genetic data, so can't help much else.

Pat

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
parts:
Everything Pat said is correct. One word of caution is using multiple imputation with 16 people... I would strongly suggest using mice to make 10-20 data sets and then pool your estimates. So the `semTools` package will be needed. You'll call growth.mi() to a mice object (that has not had mice::complete() called to it (i.e., the m = 20 data sets)). 

Anyways, I wanted to offer 3 more avenues to explore (assuming I interpret your message correctly). I am offering this because I sadly think 16 will be too small to answer your desired question. 

As a note: I am a doctoral student in a quantitative research methods PhD, but again, I'm still a student and maybe a long-time expert can suggest something I didn't think of or shoot one of these ideas down.

1) If you have 850,000 data points which are all measured at 4 time points in 16 people, you could explore nested models which treat the 16 people as "groups" with times nested inside that, and then you'd actually have 850,000 data points at 4 times which is way more than you'd need for this. But to be fully honest, I don't know if lavaan can handle 3 levels of nesting... You might have to go to an HLM-type software or Mplus. Admittedly, I did not follow you perfectly when you explained this (because I'm a social scientist) so I'm not sure if this will work for you. 

2) You could try a data reduction method. Maybe consider latent classes of these constructs (within individuals), so that you are looking at growth of fewer constructs. And although you won't have every construct mapped, you'll have a gist of how "groups" of constructs move. 

3) The most fool-proof way--but also a way publications may push against--is to simply plot these in ggplot. You could do this two ways: 
a) get the individual growth curves, ask lavaan for the parameter estimates, and get each construct's intercept and slope for each participant. You'd then take the average slope (& the standard error) across people and plot these. If SEs don't overlap, you have a rough estimate of significance.
b) do the same thing without lavaan (i.e., plot the constructs over time) and fit a linear model to it and see if SEs overlap.  

Method 1 will likely give you a headache with implementing in and interpreting from software.
Method 2 will be very hard to concretely conceptualize and explain to others you did it "right" (conceptually, I mean, not in the software).
Method 3 does not take into account other constructs so you're essentially assuming they're fully independent by using different models, and if it's biology things are rarely fully independent. But people tend to like visuals so maybe it'll be sufficient for your purposes.

As an aside, SEM (and all of frequentist statistics) is not so good with data sets where the number of variables is larger than the number of participants. If you wanted to predict something, machine learning methods like random forests or decision trees can do that, but again those are less valid for inference than prediction (and few people have implemented these in interesting longitudinal ways like you're looking for).

Good luck!
